Here me out- the concept of the movie is amazing. I understand, empathize and relate to Barry as a character and would've LOVED to see him open up and be comfortable with being vulnerable and being seen through therapy or getting help from friends and family (boy had 7 sisters). The music helps us understand his perspective and how easily he can get overwhelmed by people around him. Instead of turning it towards a pointless romance, it would have been better if it revolved around Barry and his relationships with the people already present in his life. The romance between both protagonist seemed absolutely ingenuine and you CANNOT convince me otherwise. This is the most horrifying rom com I've ever seen. I couldn't let go of the idea that one day, Barry might end up hurting Lena too, in his fit of rage. As much as I love Love, it simply is not enough to change the whole inner and psychological dynamics of a person who has spent their whole life being one way. That being said, I respect those who liked this movie but it simply wasn't for me

Barry Egan will, without question, be physically and verbally abusive to Lena over the course of their relationship, even if he really does love her. Everything we learn about Barry, from how he treats his sisters to his pathological lying to his general inability to control his emotions, points toward this. He is violent, unstable and untrustworthy—and love, for all its beauty, is a turbulent force, not a calming one. Self-control is exactly what it sounds like: it comes from the self , not from a lover. Barry's "quirky" traits would be entirely forgivably from a character standpoint if he recognized his own flaws and made any attempt to improve or mature in ways that really matter. Telling someone you want to stop crying all the time and telling someone you want to stop lying all the time are two different things, and Barry is only interested in the former. The credits rolled and all I felt was scared for Lena, a character whose sole narrative purpose is to inexplicably love Barry. Really not trying to be annoyingly contrarian here, but this was just a tough first watch in 2026. I can see why it was important to so many oddballs, introverts, quiet creative types and whatnot back in the day. Seeing a version of your own weirdness depicted, victorious, and loved is, I imagine, very affirming. But I am baffled by how many people I know identify with Barry. He simply does not deserve the good things happening to him. I want to believe that if you made this movie today, it would be broadly rejected. Undeniably beautiful filmmaking, though. Shitty L.A. never looked better. But no.

I really want to like it because the acting is great, the visuals are beautiful, the score is brilliant. I specifically enjoyed a few shots, the first appearance of the blonde guys stepping out of a car, the phone booth lighting up when Barry connects with Lena, the first kiss scene and the second when they meet at the hotel. Maybe it was his violent outbursts to his annoying but ultimately harmless sisters, maybe it's just Adam Sandler (it's not because he's great here and I loved Uncut Gems), maybe it's that his romance is unearned, I'm not sure. Unlike When Harry Met Sally or Submarine or a litany of other life affirming, love affirming films I've watched that make me cry over my beautiful boyfriend and up the ante on the yearning, this film just left me blank. It all felt so unearned and unbaked and usually I can accept that but it also touts itself as grandiose beyond its means. TL;DR — Full Review Below There are some charming moments here, but Punch-Drunk Love is built around a concept I never fully buy. The comedy constantly asks me to emotionally relate to these people while also having them behave like cartoons, and that tension never really works for me. --- The Comedy Keeps Breaking the World There are charming moments in Punch-Drunk Love, but the central concept feels pretty thin. A lot of the comedy boils down to Sandler talking like an idiot or Philip Seymour Hoffman yelling and being vulgar. That can be funny, but it creates a larger problem with the movie’s tone. PTA often uses humor in a way that seems to prioritize the joke over whether the characters still feel relatable or internally believable. These people are supposed to: A. feel psychologically real enough that I can bond with them and take their emotions seriously, B. behave with the kind of exaggerated absurdity the comedy demands, and C. still plausibly exist and function inside what is otherwise presented as the normal world. I have trouble reconciling all three. The movie doesn’t quite present itself as an outright absurd comedy, so the bizarre behavior doesn’t get the same free pass it would in something like an Adam McKay movie, where the world itself is intentionally exaggerated and logically warped. Here, I’m still being asked to emotionally invest in Barry and Lena as real people while the movie repeatedly bends human behavior around whatever joke or uncomfortable moment it wants to land. That disconnect kept me from buying into the romance or the comedy as much as I probably needed to.

To say the least, and in all honesty, it's undoubtedly one of the sweetest and most adorable films I probably have seen till then. Something about this peculiar individual, who's scared of everyone, deeply hates everyone, when a someone comes along the way, who willingly stoops down a level despite being aware of flaws- which are argued to be many. Well, it starts with lies, and continues to progress on many different levels, where truly, all those mistakes are made solely because he doesn't want to come off in a wrong way, which would've possibly led to her never coming back to him. But she accepts him for who he is, making him naturally confess many of the mistakes he had the guilt of doing. There's also this harmonium, that's rather absurdly random at first, but it's some sort of indirectly direct symbolism, that maintains itself throughout the film, it displays his levels of love rather, and its transition between being scared to even go near it, which indicates a fear of love, I presume. And towards the end, he carries it everywhere, at last, as he puts in an effort in learning the instrument, while learning to love. But that's just my guess, and I might be wrong. And Philip Hoffman, ugh, he hardly has screentime and yet literally owns every scene he's in. His breakout is just so perfect yet funny at the same time, I can't imagine anyone else at all being able to do that. Emily Watson was so nice to see, I mean, she goes through a lot, and yet its almost as if we despite knowing her little by little throughout the film, still don't know who she is completely toward the end- it's something I'm not even being able to explain. And I never imagined that I'll ever in my life see Sandler do something like this, but its clearly so effortless for him, his character knows that he can't handle himself, I'm not sure of his intentions, but from what I see, he clearly isn't willing to pour his burdens on someone that he really likes. Adam Sandler wears soothes? Yes, and he plays in a PTA movie. It’s a strong reflection on anxiety and the constant pressure to be accepted by others. PTA made a brilliant and unorthodox choice casting Sandler in this role. In my opinion, it’s his best performance and the one that represents him most truthfully. He’s known as a comedy actor and something of a clown, but he also has a real soul and genuine emotion. Those emotions come through powerfully in the scenes where color floods the screen. He cannot express his emotions and keeps everything inside, so he destroys things because he cannot control himself. That said, the story isn’t really my type. It’s a bit too dreamy, and the sudden shift from his lack of confidence to having the guts to confront the people who hurt him felt exaggerated. And somehow he knows how to fight four blond guys? I’m still not sure what that was all about. Even though there were some aspects I found incoherent, I have to give real appreciation to the cinematography, it’s still flashing in my head. The long tracking shots that move around the character, and the moments where Sandler awkwardly walks toward Lena Leonard (Emily Watson), are simply stunning. The compositions are striking.

Definitivamente está es una de mis películas de romance favoritas. No es perfecta en lo absoluto, pero tiene un alma y un corazón que te contagia durante toda la película. El personaje de Barry es (por el momento) mi protagonista favorito de la filmografía de PTA. La inocencia de Barry se ve contrastada con sus problemas de irá principalmente impulsadas por su pasado más violento. Su búsqueda de amor está obstaculizado por su inhabilidad de aceptar quien es y mentir de su pasado. Esto se ve por el como sus hermanas se comportan con el, burlandose y tratándolo como un idiota solamente por ser diferente. Inclusive si Barry les dice que no quiere hablar de esas situaciones, sus hermanas lo tratan peor por ser diferente. La carencia de comprender a Barry es lo que lo lleva a querer alejarse y volverse su propia persona. Pese a los traumas y el dolor de Barry, cuando el encuentra el amor hace todo lo posible para mantenerlo. Se da cuenta de sus errores al mentir y empieza a reconocer quién es el y que quiere hacer para mantener su amor. Hace todo dentro de su poder para proteger a quien más ama y busca el resolver sus problemas sin involucrar a nadie más. Esto hace el amor en Barry, lo convierte en una persona más genuina y capaz de hacer hasta lo imposible para buscar compañía y amor en otros. Y a través de este viaje uno puede ver las aventuras en las que Barry se encuentra y su convicción inocente para buscar ese amor verdadero. En términos de negativos, yo diría que solo Barry resplandece como personaje. Los demás personajes son muy planos y básicos, con Ledra siendo nada más que el interés romántico de Barry. Casi no se le da caracterización y, considerando que es de romance la película, uno tiene que sentir porque ese romance es importante. Aquí no se siente debido a que uno no conoce casi nada de Ledra y se ve como un personaje plano contrastando lo increíblemente escrito de Barry. A lo mejor pudieron darle más tiempo a ala película a enfocarse en Ledra y el como ella se enamora de Barry, no solo Barry de ella. Y los demás personajes son carismáticos pero no tiene mucha urgencia, y el antagonista es gracioso cuando aparece pero poco más. En general que la historia solo se enfoque en Barry crea una película bella, pero uno no puede evitar pensar que pudieron darle más tiempo para brillar a otros personajes. Para terminar, la música es tan etérea  y hermosa, apoyando al viaje de Barry. Toda la banda sonora es un deleite auditivo y hace que el amor de Barry y Ledra se convierta en real. Esto se complementa con la excelente cinematografía de PTA donde se ve lo confiado que está después de sus anteriores trabajos y como el sabe lo que quiere hacer y demostrar. Esta película me hace creer en el amor.

Wow. Wow wow wow. This film was exquisite. Despite many claims of it being an overemphasis on the mans role, or misogyny, or a focus on abelism, I believe Punch-Drunk Love is purely art. As for the beauty is within the eye of the beholder. Sure the takeaway could be that Barry the main character is an exemplified personification of what some people may view as "masculinity". He is aggressive when he's mad and physically exerts himself as an angry and destructive person. He goes after the girl, and gets her in the end. Or the takeaway could be that Anderson doesn't know how to write female characters. That Lena is used as an "incentive" to make Barry become a less destructive and weird person. However others may view it I believe that the film is subjective to the viewer. I viewed this film not through the eyes of someone who looks for strong female roles in every movie I watch, not as someone who believes aggression is only masculine, and especially not as someone who believes the meaning of something is boiled down into categories and that there is a strict line between two things. My film studies teacher taught me the word "poststructuralism". This term allows the movie to mean multiple things within itself. My diagnostic to determine whether the film was good or not was how the formalist comments evoked emotions in me. The use of; writing, acting, edition, sound, music, cinematography, and production in this film was what made me fall so deeply in love with it. Starting with the writing, there was honest comedic relief that felt natural to the story. You hear Barry and his sisters make jabs back and forth to each other throughout the film which is familiar to an audience who grew up with overbearing siblings. The acting was familiar for an Adam Sandler film, his awkward and astute wit were comforting in time of panic during the movie. Something that really pulled this film together for me and made me so intrigued as to what happened next was the sound and music of the film. With lots of percussion, weird, bizarre, and odd noises the film felt unpredictable and somewhat crazy. I believe that Punch-Drunk Love is one of my new favorite movies because I didn't expect any of it all but fell in love with the way it made me; nervous, excited, scared, cheesy, and satisfied.
